items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: I eventually came back and I started to get work which then led me to the Lionel Hampton band.

ctx.x: Well I recorded it and I left immediately for France. And while I was — no I didn’t leave for France, I went to Scotland to kind of see my family. And while I was there I was notified that I’d been awarded the New Star Award for Down Beat for doing “Twisted,” and I thought well that’s nice. But my mind wasn’t really that attuned to staying in America. And then I eventually came back and I started to get work which then led me to the Lionel Hampton band.
Okay, I had that backwards in my head. That “Twisted” came before the Hampton band.

items.title: Annie Ross — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Lionel Hampton was at Birdland... He said, 'I want you to come to Europe with me.'... In this band – it was Hamp’s band... We got to Norway. No, we got to Sweden

ctx.x: Little Benny Harris – it was owned by his mother and father, who were San Blas Indians. We were poor. Didn’t have nothin’. We shared a bathroom. Everybody was out of it. Everybody was stoned. But his mother and father were sweet. If we didn’t have money for the rent, it wasn’t a huge thing. Then we moved and stayed with John Lewis, in St. Albans, I think it was. Then Bird said, “Come on. Come and stay at my place,” which we did. Things were quiet, but we always ate. Then, what happened? I started doing solo gigs.…

He said, “I’m so sorry I’m late, but I had a meeting and I was held up.” I said, “Well, I just got out of prison.” He took me in, filled a glass – a huge glass – with whiskey. He said, “I want you to be in my show.” I said, “I don’t want to do theater.” He said, “Why?” I said, “I’ve had a couple of bad experiences, and I don’t want to do theater.
